body: Sharing E, T and J points to some similar preferences in the MBTI framework. It does not tell you whether two people want to lead a discussion, how quickly they want a decision or whether they agree on the goal.
### What the shared E, T and J each mean

Extraversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy outward, toward people, activities and the surrounding world. It gives no measure of social skill, and people who prefer Extraversion can still want time alone.

T means judgement leans more on objective, consistent standards: whether the same reason can apply to everyone, whether the conclusion has a checkable basis. It does not exclude considering people's situations; it weighs people and matters inside one set of standards that can be explained, rather than settling a conclusion directly from closeness of relationship.

Judging describes a preference for making decisions and arranging things in the external world. Preferring a clear arrangement leaves room to change the plan when information, authority or priorities change.

The three letters together guarantee neither weight in a conversation, speed of decision, strength of responsibility nor managerial competence. Whether something gets done still depends on knowledge, skill, actual authority and resources; even two people who both value arrangement can hold completely different views on the goal, the cost and the priority.
### S/N is a preference in gathering material, not a line between fact and imagination

For the same proposal, Sensing brings concrete details and relevant experience into focus: what happened, which record supports it and whether the conditions still match. Intuition gives more weight to connections between those details and possibilities that follow from them. Either person can use both kinds of information to check a proposal.

The same proposal can come from entirely different reasons. Someone supports a change because they have actually tried it once and found the old way failing under new conditions; someone supports the same change because they see a pattern not yet tested. Conversely, both may hold back for lack of evidence, or narrow the scope because the cost is too high. New is not the same as good, and familiar is not the same as reliable; whether a judgement holds depends on whether the reason can be checked and the result reviewed.
### The four-function notation used here: Te shared, second and third positions apart

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The dominant is Te for both and the inferior is Fi for both, and the difference falls on the second and third positions: one side refers to inner experience through Si and reaches outward possibility through Ne, the other integrates inner connections through Ni and meets the present situation through Se.

Te describes a theoretical leaning toward seeking logic and organisation in the outer world, Si a leaning toward referring to inner experience, and Ni a leaning toward integrating inner connections. They cannot prove reliable execution, accurate memory, good foresight or a natural fitness for leading. A shared inferior Fi does not mean both lack feeling, erupt in the same way or need the same kind of support.

The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists ESTJ’s third process as Intuition (Ne or Ni) and ENTJ’s as Sensing (Se or Si). This page uses Ne and Se in an alternating notation. That choice leaves the dominant and auxiliary processes unchanged and gives no basis for predicting what someone will do first.
### Keeping observation, comparison with experience and explanation of cause apart

"The register has slowed down" is an observation; "it was faster with the other sheet" is a comparison with experience; "duplicated circulation is causing the queue" is an explanation still to be tested. Mix the three into one sentence and the discussion becomes people talking past each other. Starting from specific facts or from a pattern are both acceptable, but either way the final questions are the same: is this information reliable, and have changes in staffing or unfamiliarity with the process been left out?

Combining the two starting points can reduce omissions, but it does not guarantee that every proposal succeeds. It has to be stated which observation would support or overturn the explanation, which old condition no longer holds, and who carries the burden of the trial. Si referring to inner experience and Ni integrating inner connections in the theory still cannot prove that someone remembers accurately, sees far or adapts better to change.

body: Scope of use: the three scenes below are original fiction written by the editors, used only to understand the trade-offs of two preferences in gathering material. They correspond to no real person or event, and cannot be used to decide which type you or anyone else belongs to.
### An original work scene: two sheets, two trials that can be tested separately

A fictional group holds a book swap. One participant writes the same title on both sheets, and the queue at the register grows. You can check the specific steps and records first, or raise the explanation of "information circulating twice" first. Writing the title twice is an observed fact; whether it is the main bottleneck, and whether it gets slower as more people arrive, still has to be checked. What each person notices first also depends on the task in their hands at the time.

Ask first what each sheet protects: one records the books received, and is the other used for returns, confirming where a book went, or correcting a mistaken pickup? If deleting one would lose the ownership information, writing it once fewer does not mean the whole is better; only if the functions really overlap is a smaller adjustment worth discussing.
There are two trials here that can be run separately, and they answer different questions.

- Clarify the instructions only: explain the division between the two sheets and the order of filling. This can answer "are comprehension and mis-filling the main problem", not "is duplicated writing the bottleneck". If the register is still slow with only the instructions changed, that is not grounds for calling duplicated circulation the main cause.
- With the necessary records and withdrawal conditions kept, reduce one duplicated entry: with staffing and attendance roughly comparable, compare the waiting time and which step jams, while keeping the original three observations — whether the instructions can be understood, whether a wrong entry can be traced back, and whether the burden has shifted onto someone else. This can answer whether duplicated writing slows the register, not whether the instructions are clear.

Both trials need withdrawal conditions agreed in advance, for example restoring the original process immediately if a book's whereabouts cannot be confirmed. If staffing is added or attendance changes markedly in the meantime, the change in speed cannot be attributed entirely to the change. When there is no improvement, go back to the judgement of cause, the instructions and the resources, rather than blaming someone for "not understanding strategy" or "resisting change". Both people can plan, check the situation and follow through, and actual skill is verified separately.
### An original relationship scene: a future benefit does not replace present consent

(A fictional scene.) A friend has already arranged an activity according to the original plan, and someone suggests replacing it with a new experience long looked forward to. Check the original agreement, the time and cost that can be carried, who has already prepared, and what the other person really wants to keep. A familiar way of doing things may feel reassuring, or may no longer suit; the new plan may be meaningful, or may only reflect the proposer's own expectation.

In this fictional outing, one line of inquiry checks the booking, refund terms and what happened on a comparable occasion. Another asks what possibilities the new outing would open up, including whether the group could try it another time. The same person can ask both questions. A possible benefit gives no authority to change someone else’s booking.

"you will like it later" cannot be treated as present consent, and "we have always done it this way" cannot be used alone to reject the other person either. You can keep the original plan, reduce the change or arrange another occasion, and state who is willing to carry what. If someone has paid or taken leave, discuss how the cancellation loss is shared; disagreeing with a new arrangement is not a lack of support, and when there is no shared willingness, not doing it is allowed.

Care in a relationship cannot be reduced to ESTJ handling the everyday and ENTJ discussing growth. Hearing a refusal, keeping an agreement and repairing an effect are individual responsibilities; a type supplies no compatibility score and cannot prove who understands the other better.
### An original pressure scene: the new display area has no owner yet

(A fictional scene.) Close to the event, the group wants to add a display area, while the existing registration and setup tasks still have no confirmed owner. List the actual commitments, the available staffing and who has authority to adjust first, then mark the addition as still to be discussed rather than as an assumed task. Before pressing for progress, check three real conditions: whether members have the material at hand, whether they have the relevant authority, and whether they have time they can commit.

In this fictional event, one line of inquiry compares actual staffing and workload with a similar display. Another proposes a different layout and asks what evidence would show whether it needs fewer people. Either person can ask both questions. Current staffing, permissions and willingness determine what can go ahead.

If nobody is both willing and able, keep the display area as a later proposal, shrink it to an acceptable scope or drop the addition, rather than substituting "everyone on the team should try harder" for an actual arrangement. State which results must be kept, which content can shrink, and which unresolved problems affect this decision, give the adjustment an owner and a way to report back, and notify the people affected.

Do not use a familiar procedure to push people into what they cannot do, and do not use long-term value to justify overload in the present. Tiredness, irritation or a shift in mood should be understood together with the burden and the support, and the inferior Fi is not used to infer the cause.

body: **Liking procedures means ESTJ.** Authority, industry norms and job training can all require specific steps; both types can also change a procedure on their own initiative, sometimes more thoroughly than anyone else.
**Talking strategy means ENTJ.** Anyone can organise a long-range plan given familiarity with a field, training in planning or a long-horizon assignment; N is not proof of strategic ability.

**S has no imagination, N is impractical.** Both preferences can use facts, models, experience and new proposals, and can switch when needed; judging intelligence or innovation by label gets it wrong in both directions.

**Voice, speed and job title.** Speaking directly, deciding quickly or sitting in a managerial post cannot determine a type and does not prove a better fitness for leading. Conversely, someone who speaks gently and listens first may also be ESTJ or ENTJ.

**Pressure reveals the real type.** Clinging to a process or overhauling a plan under deadline pressure may come from the specific risk, where the responsibility sits and how much time is left; one conflict does not prove a function out of balance or a "true face".

**Suffix and pairing.** A/T is the NERIS Identity dimension of 16Personalities, A the assertive end and T the turbulent end, covering self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure. It is not a fifth official MBTI dimension, it is unrelated to S/N, and it differs from the item bank and scoring of the FermatMind MBTI preference assessment; the two have to be read separately. A shared ETJ also guarantees neither a smooth relationship nor shared values.

body: **Framework sources.** Official MBTI describes the four preferences and their scope of use, and the type dynamics page supplies the framework of function positions; this page cites only these public explanations and no unpublished item bank or scoring detail. body: Sharing E, T and J points to some similar preferences in the MBTI framework. It does not tell you whether two people want to lead a discussion, how quickly they want a decision or whether they agree on the goal.
### What the shared E, T and J each mean

Extraversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy outward, toward people, activities and the surrounding world. It gives no measure of social skill, and people who prefer Extraversion can still want time alone.

T means judgement leans more on objective, consistent standards: whether the same reason can apply to everyone, whether the conclusion has a checkable basis. It does not exclude considering people's situations; it weighs people and matters inside one set of standards that can be explained, rather than settling a conclusion directly from closeness of relationship.

Judging describes a preference for making decisions and arranging things in the external world. Preferring a clear arrangement leaves room to change the plan when information, authority or priorities change.

The three letters together guarantee neither weight in a conversation, speed of decision, strength of responsibility nor managerial competence. Whether something gets done still depends on knowledge, skill, actual authority and resources; even two people who both value arrangement can hold completely different views on the goal, the cost and the priority.
### S/N is a preference in gathering material, not a line between fact and imagination

For the same proposal, Sensing brings concrete details and relevant experience into focus: what happened, which record supports it and whether the conditions still match. Intuition gives more weight to connections between those details and possibilities that follow from them. Either person can use both kinds of information to check a proposal.

The same proposal can come from entirely different reasons. Someone supports a change because they have actually tried it once and found the old way failing under new conditions; someone supports the same change because they see a pattern not yet tested. Conversely, both may hold back for lack of evidence, or narrow the scope because the cost is too high. New is not the same as good, and familiar is not the same as reliable; whether a judgement holds depends on whether the reason can be checked and the result reviewed.
### The four-function notation used here: Te shared, second and third positions apart

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The dominant is Te for both and the inferior is Fi for both, and the difference falls on the second and third positions: one side refers to inner experience through Si and reaches outward possibility through Ne, the other integrates inner connections through Ni and meets the present situation through Se.

Te describes a theoretical leaning toward seeking logic and organisation in the outer world, Si a leaning toward referring to inner experience, and Ni a leaning toward integrating inner connections. They cannot prove reliable execution, accurate memory, good foresight or a natural fitness for leading. A shared inferior Fi does not mean both lack feeling, erupt in the same way or need the same kind of support.

The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists ESTJ’s third process as Intuition (Ne or Ni) and ENTJ’s as Sensing (Se or Si). This page uses Ne and Se in an alternating notation. That choice leaves the dominant and auxiliary processes unchanged and gives no basis for predicting what someone will do first.
### Keeping observation, comparison with experience and explanation of cause apart

"The register has slowed down" is an observation; "it was faster with the other sheet" is a comparison with experience; "duplicated circulation is causing the queue" is an explanation still to be tested. Mix the three into one sentence and the discussion becomes people talking past each other. Starting from specific facts or from a pattern are both acceptable, but either way the final questions are the same: is this information reliable, and have changes in staffing or unfamiliarity with the process been left out?

Combining the two starting points can reduce omissions, but it does not guarantee that every proposal succeeds. It has to be stated which observation would support or overturn the explanation, which old condition no longer holds, and who carries the burden of the trial. Si referring to inner experience and Ni integrating inner connections in the theory still cannot prove that someone remembers accurately, sees far or adapts better to change.

body: Scope of use: the three scenes below are original fiction written by the editors, used only to understand the trade-offs of two preferences in gathering material. They correspond to no real person or event, and cannot be used to decide which type you or anyone else belongs to.
### An original work scene: two sheets, two trials that can be tested separately

A fictional group holds a book swap. One participant writes the same title on both sheets, and the queue at the register grows. You can check the specific steps and records first, or raise the explanation of "information circulating twice" first. Writing the title twice is an observed fact; whether it is the main bottleneck, and whether it gets slower as more people arrive, still has to be checked. What each person notices first also depends on the task in their hands at the time.

Ask first what each sheet protects: one records the books received, and is the other used for returns, confirming where a book went, or correcting a mistaken pickup? If deleting one would lose the ownership information, writing it once fewer does not mean the whole is better; only if the functions really overlap is a smaller adjustment worth discussing.
There are two trials here that can be run separately, and they answer different questions.

- Clarify the instructions only: explain the division between the two sheets and the order of filling. This can answer "are comprehension and mis-filling the main problem", not "is duplicated writing the bottleneck". If the register is still slow with only the instructions changed, that is not grounds for calling duplicated circulation the main cause.
- With the necessary records and withdrawal conditions kept, reduce one duplicated entry: with staffing and attendance roughly comparable, compare the waiting time and which step jams, while keeping the original three observations — whether the instructions can be understood, whether a wrong entry can be traced back, and whether the burden has shifted onto someone else. This can answer whether duplicated writing slows the register, not whether the instructions are clear.

Both trials need withdrawal conditions agreed in advance, for example restoring the original process immediately if a book's whereabouts cannot be confirmed. If staffing is added or attendance changes markedly in the meantime, the change in speed cannot be attributed entirely to the change. When there is no improvement, go back to the judgement of cause, the instructions and the resources, rather than blaming someone for "not understanding strategy" or "resisting change". Both people can plan, check the situation and follow through, and actual skill is verified separately.
### An original relationship scene: a future benefit does not replace present consent

(A fictional scene.) A friend has already arranged an activity according to the original plan, and someone suggests replacing it with a new experience long looked forward to. Check the original agreement, the time and cost that can be carried, who has already prepared, and what the other person really wants to keep. A familiar way of doing things may feel reassuring, or may no longer suit; the new plan may be meaningful, or may only reflect the proposer's own expectation.

In this fictional outing, one line of inquiry checks the booking, refund terms and what happened on a comparable occasion. Another asks what possibilities the new outing would open up, including whether the group could try it another time. The same person can ask both questions. A possible benefit gives no authority to change someone else’s booking.

"you will like it later" cannot be treated as present consent, and "we have always done it this way" cannot be used alone to reject the other person either. You can keep the original plan, reduce the change or arrange another occasion, and state who is willing to carry what. If someone has paid or taken leave, discuss how the cancellation loss is shared; disagreeing with a new arrangement is not a lack of support, and when there is no shared willingness, not doing it is allowed.

Sharing E, T and J points to some similar preferences in the MBTI framework. It does not tell you whether two people want to lead a discussion, how quickly they want a decision or whether they agree on the goal.

### What the shared E, T and J each mean

Extraversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy outward, toward people, activities and the surrounding world. It gives no measure of social skill, and people who prefer Extraversion can still want time alone.

T means judgement leans more on objective, consistent standards: whether the same reason can apply to everyone, whether the conclusion has a checkable basis. It does not exclude considering people's situations; it weighs people and matters inside one set of standards that can be explained, rather than settling a conclusion directly from closeness of relationship.

Judging describes a preference for making decisions and arranging things in the external world. Preferring a clear arrangement leaves room to change the plan when information, authority or priorities change.

The three letters together guarantee neither weight in a conversation, speed of decision, strength of responsibility nor managerial competence. Whether something gets done still depends on knowledge, skill, actual authority and resources; even two people who both value arrangement can hold completely different views on the goal, the cost and the priority.

### S/N is a preference in gathering material, not a line between fact and imagination

For the same proposal, Sensing brings concrete details and relevant experience into focus: what happened, which record supports it and whether the conditions still match. Intuition gives more weight to connections between those details and possibilities that follow from them. Either person can use both kinds of information to check a proposal.

The same proposal can come from entirely different reasons. Someone supports a change because they have actually tried it once and found the old way failing under new conditions; someone supports the same change because they see a pattern not yet tested. Conversely, both may hold back for lack of evidence, or narrow the scope because the cost is too high. New is not the same as good, and familiar is not the same as reliable; whether a judgement holds depends on whether the reason can be checked and the result reviewed.

### The four-function notation used here: Te shared, second and third positions apart

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The dominant is Te for both and the inferior is Fi for both, and the difference falls on the second and third positions: one side refers to inner experience through Si and reaches outward possibility through Ne, the other integrates inner connections through Ni and meets the present situation through Se.

Te describes a theoretical leaning toward seeking logic and organisation in the outer world, Si a leaning toward referring to inner experience, and Ni a leaning toward integrating inner connections. They cannot prove reliable execution, accurate memory, good foresight or a natural fitness for leading. A shared inferior Fi does not mean both lack feeling, erupt in the same way or need the same kind of support.

### Keeping observation, comparison with experience and explanation of cause apart

"The register has slowed down" is an observation; "it was faster with the other sheet" is a comparison with experience; "duplicated circulation is causing the queue" is an explanation still to be tested. Mix the three into one sentence and the discussion becomes people talking past each other. Writing one entry fewer still has to keep ownership, whereabouts, error correction and every necessary requirement; if the error is passed to someone else to trace, the total burden may not have fallen at all. The trial authorises no extra items of data collection and no public identification of participants.

If staffing is added at the same time, the change in speed cannot be attributed entirely to the instruction change. Someone with the knowledge, authority, capacity and willingness obtains the material, understands the process and actually takes on the checking, correcting and follow-up; anything nobody accepts stays on the list. If the whereabouts cannot be restored, stop the change as agreed and have the person responsible restore a workable process and notify those affected, rather than writing only "it can be withdrawn". Keep the counterexamples too: someone who checks details first proposed a new plan, someone who builds patterns first kept an old process that still worked, and a change to the instructions brought no improvement and required further investigation.
sections.title: How to keep observing yourself

items.answer:
The only letter difference is S/N. ESTJ favours concrete facts and experience, while ENTJ favours patterns, connections and possibilities. Both share E, T and J.

Take the same proposal and compare the reasons each person gives for a decision. Someone might cite comparable records or a pattern worth testing. Both can use both reasons. Check the role, information and deadline, since one action or speaking order gives no basis for typing anyone.
items.question: What is the core difference between ESTJ and ENTJ?

items.answer:
That cannot be concluded. An old method may have stopped working, and a new one may have left out a necessary condition; both types can propose change and both can keep an arrangement that works.

One workable practice is to write three things separately: whether the old conditions have changed, how the new hypothesis would be tested, and who carries the actual cost. Whether someone supports one particular change cannot type them, and innovative ability is not proved by the letter N.
items.question: Is ESTJ necessarily conservative and ENTJ necessarily innovative?

items.answer:
No. A shared dominant Te is only one arrangement within the dynamics theory, describing a leaning toward seeking logic and organisation in the outer world; it measures no managerial skill.

Actual management depends on knowledge, responsibility, authority, communication, resources and feedback on results. A shared function is neither automatic rapport nor a guarantee of reliable delivery; being forceful or assigning tasks quickly can equally cause omissions and rework.
items.question: ESTJ and ENTJ share Te, so are they equally good at managing?

items.answer:
No. In the theory Si describes referring to inner experience and Ni describes integrating inner connections; neither scores memory or foresight.

An old impression has to be checked for whether it is still accurate, and a pattern hypothesis has to state its basis and the conditions that would disprove it. A good or bad result does not directly show which function was used, and even less is it a ranking of intelligence.
items.question: Are Si and Ni memory and forecasting ability?

items.answer:
In the convention used here, ESTJ uses Ne for tertiary Intuition and ENTJ uses Se for tertiary Sensing. The Myers & Briggs Foundation also lists Ni and Si, respectively, as possible attitudes for those third processes. Both stacks end in Fi.

Whether the third position is marked inward or outward differs between tables, and this page takes the common version; that disagreement does not change the first two positions. A shared inferior also does not prove a lack of feeling, the same stress response or the same need for support, and cannot be used to infer a cause.
items.question: How do the third and inferior functions differ between the two?

items.answer:
Yes. S describes a preference in gathering material and does not restrict someone to the old ways; proposing a new approach as conditions change, and aligning steps with purpose, are not in conflict with ESTJ's preferences.

You can also look for a contrary experience: you organised the overall connections first and proposed a new direction first. Check how role, training and the material at hand influenced your starting point. One fondness for procedures, or one change to them, cannot validate a type.
items.question: Can someone who likes procedures but supports change still be ESTJ?

items.answer:
Work should not be divided by type in a fixed way. That division easily treats one person's words as high-level strategy and the other's work as execution labour, and important objections and burdens are easily lost.

A workable division follows actual knowledge, authority, time and willingness, and confirms what information the others need. Both people can set direction, check details and follow through to the end.
items.question: Should an ENTJ set the direction and an ESTJ carry it out when working together?

items.answer:
No. The original scenes and the observation exercise have not been validated against any typing threshold, and a shared ETJ or a different S/N produces no reliable compatibility score.

They can be used to discuss facts, hypotheses, needs and revision conditions. A relationship also depends on real consent, boundaries, commitments and repair; none of that is guaranteed by a few letters.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** Official MBTI describes the four preferences and their scope of use, and the type dynamics page supplies the framework of function positions; this page cites only these public explanations and no unpublished item bank or scoring detail. A/T belongs to the NERIS Identity extension of 16Personalities, A the assertive and T the turbulent end, covering self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension, and using similar letters does not mean different tests are fully equivalent.

**The four-position convention used here.** The Te–Si–Ne–Fi and Te–Ni–Se–Fi in this page are common writings, and the attitude of the third process carries a separate marking dispute; this is an editorial convention and is not claimed as the Foundation's only account. The function order describes where preference falls and does not predict the order of behaviour, a field of strength, the quality of collaboration or who is attractive.

**Editorial fiction statement.** The book swap register, the paid-for proposal for a new activity and the added display area, together with every exercise and worked example, are original educational examples. They correspond to no real person or event, constitute no medical, psychological or management advice, and cannot be used to diagnose, hire, choose a career or select a partner.

**Scope limits.** McCrae and Costa (1989) compared the 1985 MBTI with NEO-PI self and peer ratings in 267 men and 201 women aged 19 to 93; the abstract does not state whether the sample was nationally representative, and the details of sample, age, instrument version and rating source follow the original. Different tools and samples cannot be mixed. The analysis does not support true dichotomies or qualitatively distinct types, and finds overlap with some dimensions of the five-factor model, but it cannot validate the scenes here or determine anyone's type.

Erford et al. (2025) reviewed 193 studies of the English-language MBTI Form M published from 1999 to 2024. They excluded studies presented in the test manuals to keep the samples independent. They reported internal consistency estimates of 0.845–0.921 and evidence of convergence with related measures. None of the included studies provided evidence of structural validity or test–retest reliability. These findings apply to the instrument and samples studied and cannot validate NERIS A/T, the examples here or the FermatMind assessment.

This page is an educational summary based on public sources and makes no claim to independent clinical review. Revision information follows the site's version record. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screening or predicting relationships.
